title: Can AI chatbots really help shoppers find the best deals?
summary: Canadians are increasingly turning to AI chatbots to help them shop, compare items, scope out discounts and, in some cases, even make purchases. But are shoppers really seeing the best deals?

image.caption: As part of a daily alert set up by ChatGPT, Monique Welter found the smartwatch she was looking to buy for her husband — selling at a 30 per cent discount. (Hugo Levesque/CBC)

blocks.text: With Black Friday deals popping up everywhere, Monique Welter used ChatGPT to set up a daily alert to find a Garmin Instinct 3 smartwatch for less than $400.
"I was pretty shocked with the last deal it sent me because, even before Black Friday, it was 30 per cent off," she said. "Usually, famous brands don't need to go that deep in discounts."
The chatbot referred her to Sail, a Canadian outdoor equipment retailer she hadn’t even considered, which was selling the watch for $350.
Monique Welter regularly uses AI chatbots Claude and ChatGPT for wardrobe recommendations and to find Black Friday deals. (Hugo Levesque/CBC)

As the holiday shopping season ramps up, more Canadians are turning to AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Muse to help them pick a gift at a good price point. A Deloitte survey of more than 1,000 Canadians found that 39 per cent of respondents were planning to use AI to help them shop ahead of the holidays this year, including to find deals — up from 25 per cent the year before.

"We're really seeing a lot of price comparison work being done through AI chatbots, comparing between retailers, tracking the best price of a specific item across a range of retailers, and also looking for promo codes," Calgary-based retail consultant Jeff Doucette said.
But whether those bots are turning up the best prices is another question.

"It's not actually looking [through] the whole internet. It's looking for stuff that is available to AI," Montreal shopper Étienne Parent points out. "Amazon, for example, prevents bots from looking through it."
As shoppers change the way they search, buyers and businesses worry smaller shops — and potentially better deals — might be missing from their recommendations.
But AI firms and retail experts say there are ways for businesses to make sure they show up, and for consumers to find the product they're looking for.
How products get picked up by AI
Doucette says some of the best deals out there might never be picked up by chatbots.

Search engine optimization has long been a strategy for retailers, but now they're optimizing for AI search. If the shops with the best deals haven't done the work to make their websites visible to bots, retailers and consumers might both lose out.

"If you're not cited in the AI search engines, then you're not alive in the selection of choices from a consumer perspective," said Doucette, the founder and general manager of shopper research company Field Agent Canada.

Amazon released its own AI-powered assistant Alexa for Shopping earlier this month — but the e-commerce giant also quietly blocked rival AI bots from accessing information on its site. CBC News reached out to Amazon for comment, but the company did not respond.
Retail expert Jeff Doucette says consumers often use AI chatbots to compare prices and Black Friday sales across retailers, while also looking for promotional codes. (Ryan McLeod/CBC)

A recent analysis from AI research company Vaer AI and commissioned by point-of-sale and e-commerce platform Lightspeed found that AI recommendations from a number of chatbots favoured large retailers over smaller, local ones about 90 per cent of the time when relying on its own training data, and roughly half the time when live web search was enabled.
OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, told CBC News in an email that items from small businesses can show up next to options from bigger chains.

"As an example, our partnership with Shopify also helps shoppers discover products from its merchants, including small businesses, and sends shoppers directly to those stores when they click through," spokesperson Taya Christianson said.

Google, which operates Gemini, says its AI tools pull information from websites and businesses of all sizes, tapping into more than 60 billion products, including descriptions, special promotions and inventory levels.

"So if you're a retailer who is keeping your product feed in the Merchant Centre refreshed, you certainly will have the opportunity to show up," said Jamie Gargatsougias, head of retail at Google Canada.
Anthropic (which operates Claude) and Meta (Muse) did not respond to a request for comment from CBC News.
'People shop over a billion times a day and discovery on Google is applicable to businesses of all sizes,' Google Canada's head of retail Jamie Gargatsougias told CBC News. (Claude Beaudoin/CBC)
Retailers like Aldo have started to change their websites to adapt to the new ways shoppers are looking for products with AI.

The shoemaker's chief information officer, Matthieu Houle, says search used to be simple — shoppers would type in keywords, like the colour and style of shoes they were looking for, and sift through options from there.
With AI, shoppers are having a conversation with a chatbot instead.
"Now the consumers are asking more, 'Hey … I'm going to a holiday party at the office. This is what I'm gonna wear. Can you recommend me a shoe?'" Houle said.

On Aldo's end, that means providing more description about a product, as well as context about where someone might wear a pair of shoes or what to match them with, to make sure they show up in AI results.

Those changes, plus Aldo's use of Shopify's tools, which help agents and chatbots discover products, make Houle confident that Aldo is showing up in AI search. But he's not convinced by the technology’s deal-finding power just yet.
"Is [AI] a deal-hunting machine? Not in my experience so far," Houle said.
Aldo's chief information officer Matthieu Houle says AI is not quite a 'deal-hunting machine' yet. (Charles Contant/CBC)
How to find the product you want
Several retailers have launched AI-powered shopping assistants to help consumers navigate their websites.

Walmart recently launched its "Sparky" agent in Canada. Loblaw integrated its PC Express grocery delivery service with ChatGPT. Canadian Tire offers the "CeeTee" assistant to guide customers through tire comparisons, recommendations and store inventory checks.

Earlier this month, Google, in partnership with retailers including Lululemon, Shoppers Drug Mart and Simons, rolled out a new tool that lets users buy things with an AI chatbot, practically replacing the online checkout process.

Santo Ligotti, vice-president of marketing at the Retail Council of Canada, says consumers should revise their AI prompts — and the links they provide to the chatbot — to make sure they’re finding the right product at the right price. He says AI sometimes draws upon inaccurate information, fake reviews and outdated pricing.
"I think it's important to be clear about … what it is that you're asking for and making sure that you're reviewing that information," he said.
That’s something Monique Welter did when searching for a discounted smartwatch.

"I did in the beginning get a few alerts that, when I opened the link, weren't exactly the price it was saying it was," said the Toronto resident, who also uses AI to help with wardrobe recommendations.
Ligotti suggests also asking chatbots if there has been a trend of users returning the product. To state the obvious: The cheapest item may not necessarily be of the best quality.
While AI search results may not be perfect, many shoppers say chatbots save them "a lot of time" by cutting through all the Black Friday and Cyber Monday noise.
"Instead of going to five different websites, AI will do it for me in, like, three seconds," said Marc-Antoine Laporte, an avid online shopper based in Rimouski, Que.
As the old saying goes: Time is money.
